newsitem.title: UK: IEA cuts non-OPEC supply, raises demand estimates. [CORRECTED 09:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: IEA cuts non-OPEC supply, raises demand estimates. [CORRECTED 09:00 GMT]

text.p: World demand for oil in the final months of the year is likely to prove heavier than previously expected while supplies from non-OPEC producers will not rise as quickly as first thought, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Tuesday.

Global demand in the fourth quarter is now projected at 73.7 million barrels a day (bpd), a 100,000 bpd upward (corrects from downward) revision on last month's estimate, the Paris-based western energy watchdog IEA said in its monthly oil market report.
The agency revised down its previous estimate for fourth quarter non-OPEC supplies by 200,000 bpd to 45.0 million bpd, still a 1.5 million bpd rise over the third quarter.
The net result is a 300,000 bpd upward revision in the likely call on OPEC oil and stocks in the fourth quarter to 25.9 million bpd.
The IEA also revised down its estimate for third quarter non-OPEC supply by 200,000 bpd, raising its call-on-OPEC and stocks estimate by 300,000 bpd to 24.5 million.
Nevertheless, non-OPEC oil supplies still rose strongly in September, carrying world production up 900,000 bpd on the month to 72.53 million, the IEA said.
"The non-OPEC supply growth was concentrated in the UK, Norway and the US, but significant gains also occurred in China, Brazil, Canada and Mexico," it said.
"(Non-OPEC) production in Q3 96 exceeded Q3 95 levels by over 1.0 million bpd, setting the scene for a year-on-year increase of 2.3 milllion bpd in Q4 96."
For 1997 the IEA left unchanged its estimate of 1.8 million bpd global demand growth for the year on average to 73.6 million.

But its demand estimate for the first quarter 1997 was revised down 100,000 bpd to 74.7 million "with a downward revision to former Soviet Union demand more than offsetting an upward adjustment to Chinese demand."
It also shaved 100,000 bpd apiece from non-OPEC supply estimates for each of the first three quarters of next year.
Non-OPEC supply on average for next year is revised down by by 100,000 bpd to 45.5 million bpd, a rise of 1.8 million over 1996.
